This unit's irregular verbs

No new rule today: we're bringing back all the irregular verbs from this unit. Two tricks are enough to find most of the forms.

Trick 1: the loro form is built on the io form

Take the io form and replace the final -o with -ono: you get the loro form.

ioloroverb
escoesconouscire
vengovengonovenire
vogliovoglionovolere
possopossonopotere
devodevonodovere
bevobevonobere
rimangorimangonorimanere
scelgoscelgonoscegliere

The exceptions are very short verbs: vado → vanno, faccio → fanno, sto → stanno, do → danno, so → sanno.

The trap: uscire starts with e- for io, tu, lui and loro: esco, esci, esce, escono. Only noi and voi keep the u: usciamo, uscite. “Uscono” doesn't exist.

Trick 2: the voi form is almost always regular

Drop the -re of the infinitive and add -te: that's the voi form.

infinitivevoi
doveredovete
poterepotete
volerevolete
saperesapete
farefate
uscireuscite

Only one exception in this unit: bere → bevete.

“Devete” and “debbete” don't exist: dovere → dovete. The o of the infinitive only stays with voi; elsewhere you have dev- (devo, devi, deve, devono) and noi is dobbiamo. And for sapere, the first person is so, never “seppo”.

", "

Making plans to go out

With these verbs, you already have everything you need to suggest, accept, decline and set up a meeting.

To…In ItalianIn English
suggestVuoi venire? / Perché non andiamo in centro?Do you want to come? / Why don't we go downtown?
acceptSì, d'accordo! / Buona idea!Yes, OK! / Good idea!
declineNon posso, devo lavorare.I can't, I have to work.
hesitateNon lo so.I don't know.
set the timeA che ora? Facciamo alle nove?What time? Shall we say nine?
set the placeDove ci vediamo? In piazza.Where shall we meet? In the square.

After volere, potere and dovere, the infinitive follows directly, with no “to” in between, unlike English “I want to go”: voglio andare, posso venire, devo lavorare. In the first person, it's always voglio, never “vuo”.

Ci vediamo (let's meet, see you) is a very common set phrase: ci vediamo alle nove, ci vediamo in piazza.

Where? a, in, da

Vado a casa, a teatro, in centro, in piazza, in pizzeria.I'm going home, to the theater, downtown, to the square, to the pizzeria.
Stasera andiamo da Giulia.Tonight we're going to Giulia's.

To go to someone's place (or to see a professional), it's always da, never “a”, even where English says “to the”: vado da Marco, vado dal dentista (not “al dentista”).

title: Review: making plans to go out
why: Unit 3 review: the learner needed more time on common verbs. All the unit's irregular verbs come back in a real-life situation (planning a night out), targeting the learner's mistakes: uscono, seppo, devete/debbete, vuo andare, al dentista, è in orario.
